periods.activity_title: Hearing the Train: Reading and Exploring the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.157): word web on travel — modes, feelings, destinations.
Let us discuss (p.159): stanza matching, rhyming words, rhyme scheme, personification.

time_bands.activity: Open with the word web on travel (p.157). Students quickly fill in modes of transport, reasons for travel, feelings and destinations — share aloud to warm up the class to the poem's world.

Teacher reads the poem aloud expressively (p.158–159) while students follow in their textbooks; then students read chorally. Draw attention to the rhythm created by the ABAB rhyme and the repeated refrain.
Students work on 'Let us discuss' (p.159): match each main idea to its stanza, underline and record rhyming pairs from each stanza, and identify the rhyme scheme from the four options given.

Class discussion: which word personifies the train's whistle, and how does personification make the train feel alive? Take two or three student responses and close with the idea that the train is imagined, not seen.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading word web surfaces what students already associate with travel; use it to frame why the poem's speaker is drawn to any train, regardless of destination. Students often mistake 'there isn't a train goes by' as saying many trains pass — clarify that it means the opposite: no train passes, yet the speaker imagines one every time. The adventure-camp discussion questions (p.157) are rich oral warm-ups; they are not done in class today but make excellent self-study preparation for any student who wants to think more about travel before engaging the poem.
materials: Blackboard or chart for word web

periods.activity_title: Tone, Imagery and the Speaker's Heart: Deeper Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.159–160): tone words, symbolism, repetition, day-night contrast, imagery.
Let us think and reflect (p.160): extract questions on 'My heart is warm' and full-poem reflective questions.

time_bands.activity: Return to 'Let us discuss' (p.159): students choose tone words from the given list and identify what the train symbolises; brief pair-share, then whole-class consolidation. Connect tone to the poem's warm, enthusiastic mood.

Focus on the repeated refrain 'there isn't a train goes by' and the day-night contrast; students answer the contrast question (p.160) and identify imagery phrases such as 'cinders red on the sky' and 'day is loud' in pairs.

Read the extract beginning 'My heart is warm with the friends I make' (p.160) together. Students answer: what does 'heart is warm' mean, what does the speaker say about her friends, and what does 'no matter where it's going' reveal about her attitude to travel.
Brief whole-class reflection: does the poet actually see and hear the train, or is it all imagination? Invite two or three students to share their reasoning before closing the reading exploration.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud and mapped its rhyme scheme, students are ready to move from surface features to interpretation. Watch for the common confusion between the speaker's tone (warm, enthusiastic, content) and a literal reading of sadness about missing trains — the final stanza's friends and unconditional acceptance are the tonal anchor. The imagery question (p.160) covering multiple phrases is rich but time-consuming; if the class needs more time on the extract analysis, the imagery task can be noted in student books as self-study.

periods.activity_title: Listening Carefully, Speaking Clearly: Announcement and Pronunciation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.162–163): circle incorrect statements in the school-trip announcement, then correct them.
Let us speak (p.163): classify and pronounce words with hard and soft 'c' in pairs.

time_bands.activity: Set the listening context: a school morning-assembly announcement about a trip to the National Science Centre. Ask students to read the seven statements on p.162 silently so they know what to listen for.
Read the announcement transcript aloud at a measured pace (p.177). Students circle the statements they believe are incorrect as they listen. Read the announcement a second time for confirmation.

Students write the correct version of each incorrect statement (p.163). Take whole-class responses; confirm each correction against the announcement details — date, return time, refreshments, phone policy, permission-slip signatory, and the excursion in-charge's role.

Introduce the hard and soft 'c' rule from 'Let us speak' (p.163). Model the pronunciation of 'cell' and 'cable' to illustrate the contrast; students then work in pairs, pronouncing all eleven words and sorting them into hard-c and soft-c columns in their notebooks.

Pairs share their sorted lists; class compiles one agreed column chart. Invite volunteers to say a word from each column; correct mispronunciations gently and celebrate accurate attempts before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: The announcement is dense with details; students often mishear the return time (5.30, not 5.00) and the permission-slip signatory (parent, not teacher) — these are the most productive corrections to discuss. For the pronunciation activity, students who speak languages where 'c' is always hard may need an extra modelled example; 'bicycle' and 'circle' tend to be the trickiest because the 'c' appears twice with different sounds in each word.

periods.activity_title: Diamante Poem, Poetic Expressions and Sound Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.161): write a diamante poem connecting 'reading' and 'adventure'; share with class.
Let us learn (p.161): match poetic expressions to meanings; fill blanks with the expressions.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.161–162): match sound words and complete the paragraph using suitable sound words.

time_bands.activity: Read the diamante poem example ('Day / Bright, sunny / …/ Night') from 'Let us write' aloud together. Point out the diamond shape and how each line changes the word type — nouns at the tips, adjectives and -ing words building outward.

Students use the template provided in 'Let us write' to draft their own diamante poem connecting 'reading' and 'adventure'. Circulate to prompt: choose adjectives that truly contrast the two nouns, and make the middle -ing line the turning point.
Three or four volunteers read their diamante poems aloud; classmates offer one word of appreciation. Collect or display poems if space permits — this closes the writing task within the sitting.

Move to 'Let us learn' (p.161): students match each poetic expression (miles away, cinders red, heart is warm, day is loud, engine steaming) with its meaning in Column 2. Discuss each match as a class, explaining how the poem's context determines meaning.

Students fill in the five blanks using the matched expressions (p.161). Take responses aloud; confirm and briefly discuss why each expression fits its sentence before assigning the sound-words task as home study.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes write diamante poems that simply list random adjectives; nudge them to choose words that reflect the poem's own imagery of movement and warmth — 'dreaming', 'rushing', 'restless' fit the chapter's world well. The poetic-expression matching works best when students are asked to return to the poem's lines first: seeing 'day is loud with voices speaking' in context before matching it prevents guesswork. The sound-word matching and paragraph completion task (p.161–162) is assigned for home study because it is vocabulary-rich and benefits from unhurried individual attention.

periods.activity_title: India's Heritage Trains: Group Research and Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.165): group research and presentation on India's Mountain Railway UNESCO Heritage sites.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Mountain Railways of India from 'Let us explore' (p.165). Briefly name the three UNESCO World Heritage railways and the two on the tentative list, and invite students to share what they already know about any of them.

Form groups of four. Each group selects one or two heritage railways to focus on and plans its presentation: route, unique features, why it earned UNESCO status, and one interesting travel fact. Groups use their textbooks and any reference materials available.

Groups present in turn — a quick two-minute share per group. Audience members listen for one new fact per presentation and note it down. Teacher facilitates with a guiding question after each group if time permits.

Brief whole-class reflection: which heritage train would the class most like to travel on, and why? Connect student responses back to the poem's theme — the joy of going 'no matter where it's going' — to close the chapter on the poem's spirit.

periods.teacher_notes: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway is the most familiar to students; encourage groups to take less well-known railways (Nilgiri, Kangra Valley) so that presentations add new knowledge for everyone. The poem's unconditional longing for travel — 'no matter where it's going' — is the thread that ties the project to the literary experience; returning to that line in the closing reflection makes the connection explicit without forcing it. The second beyond-text task on Vande Bharat and underwater rail tunnels (p.165) is a rich optional extension for interested students to pursue independently.
materials: Reference books or printed fact sheets if available

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 158 beginning "The railroad track is miles away." Which of the following best describes the rhyme scheme of this stanza?

options.label: A
options.text: AABB — the first two lines rhyme with each other and the last two rhyme with each other.

options.label: B
options.text: ABAB — alternate lines rhyme: the first with the third, and the second with the fourth.

options.label: C
options.text: ABBA — the first line rhymes with the fourth, and the second with the third.

options.label: D
options.text: ABCA — only the first and third lines rhyme; the second and fourth do not share a rhyme.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be counting line-end sounds without tracking alternation — pairing lines 1–2 and 3–4 rather than 1–3 and 2–4.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student recognises that non-adjacent lines rhyme but reverses the pattern, placing the outer pair first rather than the alternating pair.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly identifies that lines 1 and 3 rhyme but misses the second rhyming pair entirely, treating the scheme as partial.

items.source_context: Millay's 'Travel': ABAB rhyme scheme, personification of whistle, stanza-idea matching, imagery phrases, day-night contrast, speaker's tone and train symbolism.
items.item_stem: In the poem 'Travel,' the speaker is equally haunted by the train during the busy day and the silent night. What does this contrast between day and night reveal about the nature of the speaker's longing for travel? Support your answer with at least one image from the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The contrast shows that the speaker's longing is constant and all-consuming — neither the noise of the day ('day is loud with voices speaking') nor the stillness of sleep can silence it. The train's whistle by day and its glowing 'cinders red on the sky' by night together suggest that the desire to travel is not triggered by boredom or circumstance but lives permanently in the speaker's imagination.

items.item_stem: Listen to the school announcement about the trip to the National Science Centre. Which of the following statements about the announcement is TRUE?

options.text: Students are permitted to carry a notebook and a pen to make notes.
Students are required to return to school by 5.00 in the evening.
The permission slip must be signed by the class teacher.
The trip to the National Science Centre will be held on 16 September.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the announcement states 16 September.
2. False — students return by 5.30 in the evening, not 5.00.
3. True — the announcement explicitly permits a notebook and pen for notes.
4. False — the permission slip must be signed by the parent, not the class teacher; it is submitted to the class teacher.

items.source_context: School-trip announcement to National Science Centre: date, timings, dress code, permitted items, permission-slip details, excursion in-charge.
items.item_stem:
After listening to the announcement about the trip to the National Science Centre, a student made the following notes. Two of the details are wrong. Identify the two incorrect details and write the correct information for each.

(1) The trip departs from school at 8.00 a.m. and students return by 5.00 p.m.
(2) Students may carry jewellery and mobile phones if they wish.
(3) Mr. Mukherjee is the excursion in-charge for the trip.
(4) Light refreshments will be provided at the museum.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Detail 1 is incorrect: students return by 5.30 p.m., not 5.00 p.m. Detail 2 is incorrect: students are NOT permitted to wear jewellery or carry mobile phones.

items.source_lo: Student applies phonological rules to pronounce words accurately using guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Hard and soft 'c' pronunciation rule applied to words: cell, cable, race, cake, decide, receive, concert, circle, bicycle, echo, uncle.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read aloud the following words from the 'Let us speak' activity. After each word, say aloud whether the 'c' in that word is a hard 'c' sound (as in 'cat') or a soft 'c' sound (as in 'city'), and briefly explain why, using the rule about which letters follow 'c'. Words: cable, receive, concert, circle, echo.

expected_elements: States the correct sound for each word: cable /k/, receive /s/, concert /k/, circle /s/, echo /k/.
Links the sound to the rule: hard before a, o, u or consonant; soft before e, i, y.
Pronounces each word clearly and at a natural pace.
Corrects self if mispronounced, showing awareness of the rule.

items.source_lo: Student applies phonological rules to pronounce words accurately using guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Hard and soft 'c' pronunciation rule applied to words: cell, cable, race, cake, decide, receive, concert, circle, bicycle, echo, uncle.
items.item_stem: The word 'bicycle' from the 'Let us speak' activity contains the letter 'c' twice. In a short spoken response of two to three sentences, explain how the hard and soft 'c' rule applies to both occurrences of 'c' in 'bicycle', and give one other word of your own choice where the same contrast appears within a single word. Be ready to pronounce both words.

expected_elements: Correctly identifies the first 'c' in bicycle as hard /k/ (before y treated as vowel but preceded by 'bi-' — accept /k/ before 'y').
Correctly identifies the second 'c' in bicycle as soft /s/ (before 'le', consonant cluster — accept either analysis; award credit for noticing it sounds /s/).
Provides a plausible original example of a word with both hard and soft 'c'.
Pronounces 'bicycle' and the chosen word accurately.

items.source_context: Diamante poem connecting 'reading' and 'adventure' using adjectives and -ing words in diamond shape.
items.item_stem: Using the diamante poem template you practised in class, write a diamante poem that moves from 'morning' to 'night'. Your poem must follow the seven-line diamond structure: line 1 is one noun, lines 2 and 6 are two adjectives each, lines 3 and 5 are three -ing words each, line 4 is a four-word phrase capturing the turn from one noun to the other, and line 7 is the contrasting noun. Choose adjectives and -ing words that reflect the mood of each time of day.

expected_elements: Follows the seven-line diamante structure correctly.
Adjectives and -ing words reflect the mood of morning and night.
Line 4 phrase creates a meaningful transition between the two nouns.
Spelling and capitalisation are consistent throughout.

items.item_stem: In Millay's poem 'Travel,' the speaker loves travel so much she would take any train, no matter where it goes. Write a short creative paragraph (80–100 words) imagining you are the speaker of the poem and you have just boarded a train to an unknown destination. Describe what you feel and what you imagine you might discover. Use at least two vivid images in your paragraph.

expected_elements: Written from the first-person perspective of Millay's speaker.
Includes at least two vivid sensory or visual images.
Conveys enthusiasm or openness about an unknown destination.
Paragraph is within the 80–100 word range and uses correct punctuation.

items.item_stem: Match each poetic expression from 'Travel' in Column A with the experience or image it best captures in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A — Expression | Column B — What it captures
miles away | The distant, unreachable quality of something desired
cinders red | Glowing sparks or embers lighting up a dark sky
heart is warm | A feeling of deep affection or gratitude toward others
day is loud | The busy, noisy energy of daytime activity
engine steaming | The powerful, forceful motion of a moving machine

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: miles away – The distant, unreachable quality of something desired; cinders red – Glowing sparks or embers lighting up a dark sky; heart is warm – A feeling of deep affection or gratitude toward others; day is loud – The busy, noisy energy of daytime activity; engine steaming – The powerful, forceful motion of a moving machine.

answer_key.right: The distant, unreachable quality of something desired
Glowing sparks or embers lighting up a dark sky
A feeling of deep affection or gratitude toward others
The busy, noisy energy of daytime activity
The powerful, forceful motion of a moving machine

items.source_context: Poetic expressions from 'Travel': miles away, cinders red, heart is warm, day is loud, engine steaming — meanings and blank-fill usage.
items.item_stem: The expressions from Millay's poem can be used beyond the poem itself. Choose any TWO of the five expressions (miles away, cinders red, heart is warm, day is loud, engine steaming) and write one original sentence for each, in a context that has NOTHING to do with trains or travel. Your sentences must show that you understand what each expression means.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Answers will vary. Accept any two sentences that use the chosen expressions correctly and in a non-travel context — for example, using 'heart is warm' to describe gratitude after receiving help, or 'day is loud' to describe a busy marketplace. The test is whether the expression's core meaning (affection, brightness, noise, power, distance) is preserved in the new sentence.

items.source_context: Mountain Railways of India — Darjeeling Himalayan, Nilgiri, Kalka-Shimla (UNESCO); Matheran Hill, Kangra Valley (tentative list).
items.item_stem: Working in a group of four, prepare a short presentation (five to six slides or a poster) on ONE of the Mountain Railways of India listed in 'Let us explore' (p.165). Your presentation must cover: (1) the route and states it passes through, (2) the features that make it unique, (3) why it was awarded or is being considered for UNESCO World Heritage status, and (4) one personal reflection — would you like to travel on this railway, and why? Present your findings to the class.

expected_elements: Covers route, uniqueness, and UNESCO status with accurate facts.
Presentation is clearly organised and easy to follow.
Personal reflection connects to the poem's theme of travel.
Each group member contributes visibly to the presentation.

items.source_lo: Student researches and presents on a real-world topic extending the poem's theme using project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Mountain Railways of India — Darjeeling Himalayan, Nilgiri, Kalka-Shimla (UNESCO); Matheran Hill, Kangra Valley (tentative list).
items.item_stem: After hearing the group presentations on India's Mountain Railways, write a comparison of any two heritage railways your class discussed. In your comparison, address: (a) what makes each railway distinctive, (b) which of the two you would choose to travel on and why, and (c) how travelling on either of these railways connects to the spirit expressed in Millay's poem 'Travel' — the joy of going 'no matter where it's going.'

expected_elements: Compares two railways with at least one specific distinguishing feature each.
States a personal preference with a reasoned explanation.
Connects the chosen railway's appeal to the poem's theme of unconditional wanderlust.
Written in clear paragraphs with accurate spelling and punctuation.
